stories.title: This Indian pilgrim was about to enter Tibet for her dream tour - then her WhatsApp messages stopped
stories.summary: Early on Wednesday, Sudipto Bhattacharya received what would be the last messages from his wife. She'd sent a picture of a departure stamp in her passport at 07:57 (02:27 GMT) - immigration at the Nepal border was done. Six minutes later, at 08:03, she wrote: we are waiting to enter China. Subhrasree Chakraborty and the group she was travelling with had been waiting to cross into Tibet for the next stage of their pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, the sacred Himalayan home of Hindu god Shiva that Subhrasree had dreamed of visiting for years. The 43-year-old is now among at least 290 Indians reported missing after deadly flash floods struck along Nepal's border with Tibet. Many of those unaccounted for were on the pilgrimage, which resumed last year after being disrupted by the pandemic and then by tensions between India and China. Several thousand Indians have been making their way to Mount Kailash for years. Subhashree was travelling without her family, as part of a group of about 30 people. A medical technologist working in critical care at a city hospital, Subhrasree was used to emergencies. She knew CPR and intensive-care procedures and, according to her husband, was physically fit. But none of that has brought her husband Sudipto Bhattacharya any closer to knowing what happened after that final message. "After 08:03am, what happened?

stories.title: Parliament's support for Arctic demonstrates new approach to North's development
stories.summary: More than 1,000 Arctic projects are worth more than $407 billion investment
article_sentences: MURMANSK, August 28.

The fact that the United Russian Party's public program now contains a special Arctic section demonstrates the parliamentary support for projects related to development of the northern territories and a change in the state approach: from initiatives to arrangement of processes at the legislative level, Doctor of Economics, leading the Expert Council on Arctic Development at the St. Petersburg Committee on Foreign Relations Alexey Fadeev told TASS.
"The fact that there is now an Arctic section demonstrates that the state policy related to development of the northern territories and the Arctic is approaching a fundamentally new level," he said.
"We have used to live having, so to say, some initiatives and proposals.

Some things, of course, have been implemented at a certain level, and legally fixed, but the fact that such a section now is part of the United Russia Party's program guarantees a systematic approach to legislative support for projects aimed at the Arctic's development."
The Arctic is an indisputable way of developing the Russian economy, he stressed.
Right now, there are more than 1,000 Arctic projects with a total investment of more than 35 trillion rubles ($407 billion).
One in six rubles in the Russian economy is formed in the Russian Federation's Arctic Zone, which is about 15% of GDP and 25% of exports.
Moreover, the expert continued, with the developing logistics projects, the Arctic's growth potential is huge.
"The Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor, the Northern Sea Route, the building of new icebreakers, the construction of infrastructures, the upgrade of ports and railways," the expert said.

"However, we must remember that the Arctic is not just tons of oil, cubic meters of LNG or certain amounts of extracted ore, since, above all, it is about people, and therefore a significant emphasis in the section is placed on the social aspect.
Those are aspects of retaining people in the northern territories as well as of attracting new, highly qualified personnel: engineers, doctors, and teachers.

stories.title: GPS collars making shepherds' lives 'much easier'
stories.summary: GPS collars are changing the way animals grazing on Jersey's cliffsides are managed, local shepherds have said. Conservation initiative The Grazing Project has pioneered use of the collars on large flocks of sheep, with its efforts so successful it is now training four grazing cows to use the collars too. In 2025, the technology was featured on Clarkson's Farm, Jeremy Clarkson's fly-on-the-wall documentary about his Cotswolds farm Diddly Squat, where it was used to contain his herd of goats. Jersey brothers and shepherds Josh and Ben Voak, who work with the project, said it had saved them hours of manual labour and opened up new areas for flocks to graze. The collars use GPS technology to keep livestock within an invisible boundary drawn using a smartphone app. If the animals reach the edge of the boundary the collar delivers an audio warning and then delivers mild electric shocks. The technology was created in Norway and has been tested extensively across the UK. The project uses the collars to manage about 600 sheep in Jersey. Josh said: "We got our first 70 collars about three years ago now, since then we've been getting more and more because it makes our job so much easier. "It means we can graze more challenging areas, so steep cliffs, areas with heavy bracken or gorse... it means we can also track the sheep as well, so every day when we go looking and counting the sheep we've got them already on the app and we can find them very easily." "We used to lay electric fencing before the GPS collars came in," he added.
